First-author publication

Learning-enabled signal recovery for optical photonic ADCs

A power- and sampling-rate-agnostic learning pipeline that recovers high-fidelity signals from a nonlinear photonic time-stretch front end.

Case study

Recover the signal without retraining for every operating point.

Photonic ADCDeep learningCalibrationSignal recovery

The problem

Photonic time-stretch analog-to-digital converters can capture extremely high-bandwidth signals, but real front ends introduce nonlinear distortion through electro-optic modulation, optical filtering, dispersion, photodetection, and electronic digitization. A correction model tied to one input power or sampling rate is difficult to deploy.

The approach

The work separates the recovery problem into stages so the learned representation focuses on system distortion rather than memorizing one acquisition setting. Training data are built from known reference signals passed through the physical front end, and the recovered waveform is evaluated with communication-grade signal-quality metrics.

Reported signal qualityincreasing recovery quality

The final system reached a reported 63 dB signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio and 10.18 effective bits. The architecture is designed to remain useful across sampling rates and input powers, reducing the need for repeated retraining.

My contribution

As first author, I worked across the research arc: system modelling, data generation, learning architecture, experimental evaluation, and the paper. The project was also selected among the top undergraduate projects at IIT Madras’s Electrical Engineering Research Scholars’ Symposium.

Takeaway

Learning becomes much more deployable when it encodes the invariances the physical system actually needs. The result is less a generic neural post-processor and more a calibrated component of the signal chain.
